doc.title: Web Service APIs
doc.paragraph: There are two primary ways to interact with Adaptive Framework over the network. The traditional RESTful way allows you to send standard HTTP operations to the server and get status and results back with the appropriate content-type. This method is uri-based, like a typical RESTful service and the HTTP operations map onto the adapter_session interface methods. Using the RESTful interface is particularly useful for web-based applications that are accustomed to RESTful ways to interact with object data.

section.title: REST
section.paragraph: The following table describes each HTTP Request and its corresponding adapter session method that is invoked:

HTTP GET requests act as both get_object() and retrieve_objects() adapter session calls, depending on the HTTP URI that is specified. All HTTP URIs must specify an adapterId. When an Object Type and Object Id are also supplied, the GET is treated as a get_object(). When just the adapterId and Object Type are specified, the GET request is treated as a retrieve_objects() call.

For retrieve_objects() calls, you may also specify a query criteria, which is passed along to the retrieve_objects(). This is useful if you need to narrow down the results of the retrieve_objects(), or use an index to obtain performance. The query string is URL encoded RQL, for example GET /lmdb/Person/?sn=Hopper or GET /lmdb/Person/?and(eq(dept,ENG),ge(age,40)). See the Indexes chapter of the Administrative Guide for how queries use indexes.

A relation can be written as a function, ge(age,40), or with an operator between the property and the value, age=ge=40; dept=ENG is short for dept=eq=ENG. Lists go in parentheses and are separated by commas only, as in dept=in=(ENG,OPS) or n=out=(-1,2). A query string may also hold one sort() and one select(), joined to the filter with &:

Every value in a query string is text, and is compared as the data type the object type gives the property, so age=ge=40 compares numbers when age is declared an integer. A relation on a property an object does not have is false for that object. Characters the query string uses for itself must be percent encoded in a value, including +, which is written %2B: name=in=(a%2Bb,c) is the list a+b, c. A query string the server cannot read fails with syntax (HTTP 400), for example Expecting ',' or ')' in list.

For both GET requests, you may additionally specify object options to instruct the server on how to construct the object or objects that are being returned. For a complete list of options, see the Object Type description for _AdaptiveObjectOptions_.
Adaptive Framework can be configured for a variety of content types, each of which can be used in the RESTful request/response by specifying the appropriate value for the HTTP Header Content-Type.

It's very easy to demonstrate how to use the RESTful API, using the command-line tool, curl. If you are running afwfcgi and have Apache or Nginx setup on the traditional Secure HTTP port 443, and you wanted to get the object afw of type _AdaptiveAdapter_, from the core adapter, afw, and you wanted it to be formatted with whitespace, you could run the following:

A journal adapter's entries are the object type _AdaptiveJournalEntry_. A GET of an entry's cursor returns that entry, and the journal functions are available as GETs of special object ids, each doing what the journal function of the same name does:
section.code: GET /journal/_AdaptiveJournalEntry_/get_first GET /journal/_AdaptiveJournalEntry_/get_by_cursor:<cursor> GET /journal/_AdaptiveJournalEntry_/get_next_after_cursor:<cursor> GET /journal/_AdaptiveJournalEntry_/get_next_for_consumer:<consumerId>[:<limit>] GET /journal/_AdaptiveJournalEntry_/get_next_for_consumer_after_cursor:<consumerId>:<cursor>[:<limit>] GET /journal/_AdaptiveJournalEntry_/advance_cursor_for_consumer:<consumerId>[:<limit>] GET /journal/_AdaptiveJournalEntry_/mark_consumed:<consumerId>:<cursor>
section.paragraph: A consumer form without a limit has no limit, and a limit must be 1 or more. The : does not need to be encoded. The Authorization chapter of the Administrative Guide describes how these requests are checked.
When a request fails, the response's HTTP status comes from the error's id, the same id a script sees as e.id in a catch. These are the ones a client meets most often:

row.column: A query string, object path or script that cannot be parsed
A query criteria object or modify body that is not valid
A script throw, or a function given the wrong arguments
No such adapter, object type or object
An HTTP method the resource does not allow
The request went past a limit, such as limitRequestPoolBytes
A request Content-Type the server has no content type for
An operation the adapter does not have, such as a retrieve of journal entries

section.paragraph: A model's on* script can choose the status by giving its throw an id, such as throw "Person not found" id "not_found"; for a 404. The Language Reference describes the ids a script may throw.

section.title: Perform Actions
section.paragraph: The second way to interact with Adaptive Framework remotely is to send HTTP POST payloads to the core adapter and specify which adaptive functions and parameters you'd like to interact with. This method requires clients to generate and receive payloads, but it offers some functionality that's not available through traditional REST. For example, you can invoke any adaptive function through, not just adapter session ones. To use this technique, simply use HTTP POST actions to the Core adapter, afw, along with a payload to instruct the server which adaptive function to invoke and all of its parameters.

section.title: Examples
section.paragraph: The following section provides some code samples for how to use a tool such as CURL to interact with adaptive framework by creating, modifying and and retrieving objects in different ways.
section.code: curl -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -H 'Accept: application/json' \ -X POST http://localhost/vault/users \ -d @- <<EOF { "firstName": "John", "lastName": "Doe", "email": "john.doe@myorg.org" } EOF

curl -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -H 'Accept: application/json' \ -X PUT http://localhost/vault/users/1234567890 \ -d @- <<EOF { "firstName": "Joe", "lastName": "Doe", "email": "joe.doe@myorg.org" } EOF

curl -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -H 'Accept: application/json' \ -X POST http://localhost/vault/users/1234567890 \ -d @- <<EOF [ [ "set_property", "firstName", "John" ], [ "remove_property", "lastName", "email" ] ] EOF
